assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices turned textbook many-body models (Hubbard, Mott transition, superfluid-insulator crossover) into controllable laboratory systems, so that quantum matter can be watched with single-site resolution. It is fundamental, unexpectedly clean and answers questions about how strongly correlated quantum systems behave. Its reach into condensed matter, quantum information and precision physics is broad.
assessment.attribution: The theory proposal (Jaksch, Zoller and collaborators) and the first Mott-insulator realisation (Greiner, Bloch, Hansch) are the decisive steps; quantum-gas microscopy and later developments widen the field. The list has five names and Cirac, Esslinger are also strong, so any trio leaves out important contributors. I pick one theory and two experimental names, but this is a judgement call.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of independent confirmation across many laboratories, with quantitative theory-experiment agreement. The field is mature and the recognition is not premature.
uncertainties: Which three of five credited names is unresolved; Hansch, who is not on the credited list, also bears on the original experiment.
I rely on my recollection of the history and have not verified the detailed priority claims.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks at the 10^-18 level are a precision-measurement achievement of the first rank. The magic-wavelength idea is simple and elegant, and the clocks test relativity at the millimetre scale and open new tests of fundamental constants. As an atomic theorist I value results where theory and measurement agree to such precision.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and realised the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group pushed systematic uncertainty and coherence to record levels. Two names give a clean configuration. Others (Lemonde, Hall, Hansch comb context) may argue for a role.
assessment.maturity: Several independent groups (JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) reproduce and improve the results, and clock comparisons are routine. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so recognition may come either now or later.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a prize for a technology advance rather than a discovery about nature; it is close to the 2005 and 2012 prizes in theme.
Credit split with the earlier frequency-comb and ion-clock work is partly outside the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal and its experimental realisation with trapped ions established the first working quantum gates, entanglement of many particles, and digital and analogue quantum simulation. This is a foundational result on controlling single quantum systems and it connects directly to my own field of atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller provided the theory; Blatt's group demonstrated gates, entangling operations and simulation at scale. This trio is natural. Wineland was recognised in 2012 for ion control, so the new prize should clearly rest on quantum computation and simulation, which is a distinct contribution.
assessment.maturity: The experiments have been repeated by many groups for over twenty years and are mature. Scalable computing is still developing, but the physics underlying it is secure.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with other candidates that list Cirac and Zoller (B020 and B040); credit would need to be balanced across entries.
Other experimental groups (Monroe, Wineland, Innsbruck and NIST) have strong claims that are not on this entry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The BEC-BCS crossover gave a clean, tunable realisation of a strongly interacting fermionic superfluid, with universal behaviour linking neutron-star matter, superconductors and cold atoms. It is fundamental and shows nature behaving in a surprisingly universal way.
assessment.attribution: Grimm, Salomon and Thomas each had decisive early experiments (molecular BEC, collective modes, thermodynamics). The list omits Jin and Ketterle, who are central to the experimental history; I follow the supplied credit only. Theory contributions (Leggett, Nozieres-Schmitt-Rink and others) are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Many independent measurements and quantitative agreement with Monte Carlo theory; thoroughly mature. Timing is acceptable but not urgent.
uncertainties: The absence of Deborah Jin (deceased) and Wolfgang Ketterle among credited names makes the configuration questionable.
Unclear whether the discovery adds enough beyond the 2001 BEC prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED reproduced atom-photon interaction in a solid-state circuit and gives strong coupling, dispersive readout and the architecture of superconducting quantum processors. It is original and has had enormous reach.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf (with Wallraff, Majer and others) proposed and demonstrated the architecture; four credited names must become three. I choose the experimental pair plus the theory proposer, but Girvin's role is also key.
assessment.maturity: It has been confirmed in many laboratories, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is recent and the committee may be wary of a close follow-up so soon.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
Which of Blais and Girvin deserves the theory slot is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry uses the wave nature of matter for measurements of gravity, rotation and fundamental constants. It is a conceptually direct demonstration of quantum mechanics with a wide range of precision applications.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard and Bordé established the first atom interferometers and the theoretical framework; Kasevich made the precision gravimeters and gyroscopes. Chu (a Nobel laureate in 1997 for cooling) and Schmiedmayer also carry weight, and four names compete for three places.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with many groups and field-deployed instruments. The discovery was gradual rather than a single event, which makes clear attribution harder.
uncertainties: Diffuse credit and overlap with the 1997 prize and the 2022 quantum-information prize themes.
Whether recent tests of fundamental physics have reached a decisive result.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase reveal that potentials and geometry have physical consequences in quantum mechanics, a conceptual insight that underlies topological matter. It is the kind of unexpected, deep result about nature I find compelling.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov (with Bohm, who is not credited here and is deceased) and Berry are the two natural names. The credited list supports a fair two-person prize, though Bohm's priority for the 1959 paper cannot be recognised.
assessment.maturity: Fully confirmed for decades through electron holography, interferometry and molecular physics. The recognition is late rather than premature, but a committee may judge the effects as already honoured indirectly through topological prizes.
uncertainties: Bohm's omission, and whether Pancharatnam or Longuet-Higgins precedents affect priority of the geometric phase.
Whether the committee views this as a discovery or a theoretical insight.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought mechanical oscillators to their quantum ground state and to squeezed and entangled states, addressing the boundary between the quantum and classical worlds. I find this question compelling, and the measurements underpin gravitational-wave detectors.
assessment.attribution: Aspelmeyer, Kippenberg and Painter led the key demonstrations of cooling, strong coupling and quantum-state control; Cleland also demonstrated mechanical ground-state cooling. Four names must be reduced to three.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by several groups, though the field is still developing and much of the strongest evidence is recent. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects gives context but may also lessen the novelty.
uncertainties: Whether the field has yet produced a result that is clearly decisive on the quantum-classical boundary.
